facts_from_discussion: Petitioner did not argue or establish that the burden of proof shifts to respondent under section 7491(a).

Petitioner asked the Court to determine that his state and local general sales tax deduction is $1,456; the Notice of Deficiency allowed $1,466, $10 more; the parties do not dispute that the allowed amount was calculated using the IRS optional sales tax tables for 2020.

Respondent agrees that the Notice of Deficiency's explanatory statement that taxable income was 'increased $6,884' is inaccurate; the adjustment reduced the total itemized deduction for state and local taxes.
Petitioner failed to keep receipts or other proof to substantiate a state and local sales tax deduction beyond what the IRS allowed.

On brief petitioner did not dispute the amount of gambling losses the IRS allowed ([REDACTED AMOUNT]), less than the $30,100 he claimed; at trial he argued his winnings were less than reported and less than the allowable losses.

Petitioner asserts his 2020 gambling income was only $12,221, relying on documents not admitted into evidence; he first testified at trial that he and his spouse won only $12,221 and that losses exceeded that amount.
The gambling winnings and losses in the record appear to be his spouse's; she is not a party and did not testify; petitioner testified he used an estimate of $30,000.
The admitted casino win-loss statements and testimony do not present a clear picture of 2020 gambling winnings or losses; no Forms W-2G or other information returns reported the winnings.
The Court did not find petitioner's testimony as to his asserted gambling winnings credible; he kept no diary or verifiable documentation.
Petitioner did not provide a reasonable basis to estimate his 2020 gambling winnings at less than the $30,100 reported.
Petitioner did not demonstrate gambling losses greater than the amount the IRS allowed ([REDACTED AMOUNT]).
The Civil Penalty Approval Form was approved and signed by a supervisory tax specialist who affirmed being the examiner's immediate supervisor, acting supervisor, or designated higher level official.
Petitioner prepared his own return and appears to have simply guessed at the gambling winnings and losses he reported.
The Court found petitioner failed to maintain adequate records to calculate his tax liability and did not show reasonable cause and good faith.
